This article reports on a Databricks hackathon built around the product Lakebase, described as fully managed Postgres that is storage-separated from compute and governed by Unity Catalog alongside lakehouse data. The event opened to more customers than previous years and ran two tracks with eleven customer projects: Track 1 focused on branching and building applications; Track 2 focused on syncing and serving. Under both tracks, Unity Catalog governs access whether the data is queried in a notebook or read by a production app.

Track 1 targeted application developers who build apps, APIs, and agents on operational data. Every Lakebase project starts with a production branch, and child branches are created instantly using copy-on-write storage so only changed data consumes new storage and creating a branch has no performance impact on production. Teams used Genie Code to build their apps and treated branches as cheap, disposable copies of production.

Lyft built Jevons Search for AI agents that issue refunds, cancel bookings, or close tickets without knowing database business rules embedded in triggers. For each batch of support tickets the agent forks a copy-on-write branch of production in about six seconds, applies its actions, reads back what the database did, and adjusts; instead of using a large LLM to plan, a lightweight classifier built on gte-large embeddings tracked in MLflow and served on Model Serving sorts each ticket into one of eight policy categories with no LLM tokens used at runtime. On a synthetic dataset from Wanderbricks sample data, planning up front fully resolved 2 of 11 support backlogs within policy, while testing on branches resolved 10 of 11; the team also found that Lakebase forked fast enough to score more than four times as many branches in the same minute, but more branches did not lead to more passes. CIBC built Branchflight so every pull request gets its own preview environment: it creates a zero-copy Lakebase branch from a PII-masked template branch in under five seconds and deploys a preview Databricks App connected to it; environments scale to zero when unused, expire automatically after a set time, pass through a schema-diff check before merging, and the platform's own state, audit logs, and cost metrics live in Lakebase. Arbital Health built 7NF (seven normal forms), which keeps data fixed while changing the schema with each layout running as its own Lakebase branch to test how much the schema affects text-to-SQL accuracy.

Branching appeared elsewhere: OneTrust treated firewall rules like code, spinning up a copy-on-write Lakebase branch with dedicated compute and connecting a test instance to run recursive reachability queries and policy checks so trial runs that expanded attack surface were discarded instantly while validated rules merged into production. A second CIBC team built BranchCut, a 3D cinematic workspace bringing Git-style branching and merging to creative work. Reach Mobile built StreetCart for comparing nearby stores on price, distance, and stock, using Lakebase as the operational database for products, stores, and inventory with Lakebase search powering product discovery.

Markel served reads from property and casualty insurers—claims analysts searching policies by number, name, address, or phone; call center agents identifying callers by phone across policy, claims, and broker data; underwriters seeing loss runs per broker—and scored new claims for risk as they arrived. Instead of a separate search index like Elasticsearch with its own pipeline, schema drift, and governance gaps, Markel served those reads from the same governed gold tables used for analytics through Lakebase.

Track 2 targeted data and ML engineers who build pipelines and models that usually need a separate path to reach apps needing milliseconds. Synced tables move curated Unity Catalog data into Lakebase Postgres as read-only tables via managed Spark Declarative Pipelines; Lakehouse Sync (change data capture) replicates Postgres changes back into Unity Catalog Delta for analytics; and Databricks Online Feature Stores run on Lakebase so features defined in the lakehouse can be served to models in real time.

Data Axle built PriceWise across more than 18,000 listings, estimating hosts leave about 64% of potential nightly revenue on the table. It combines hybrid search (pgvector embeddings plus BM25 merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion), pricing suggestions broken into four demand drivers including PostGIS comparisons within 20 miles, and an embedded Genie agent whose conversations are saved in Lakebase as agent memory; all run from one Lakebase database kept current through synced tables, with pricing responses in as little as 4 milliseconds. A transportation company built a real-time flight risk app syncing flight, airport, and weather alert tables into Lakebase to power a live map in a Databricks App. An insurance team scored post-bind inspection likelihood and ranked the queue so the riskiest policies are seen first with plain-language reasons, using features defined once as Databricks Feature Views served from a Lakebase online store.

Sobeys built a conversational shopping assistant with three agents: a recipe agent finding recipes via Vector Search, a product agent matching ingredients to products using fuzzy Postgres trigram search, and a health agent checking every recipe against family allergy profiles. The article concludes that the same Unity Catalog governance applies to lakehouse tables and the Postgres tables serving them, so several teams replaced separate systems—search indexes, staging databases, or hand-built sync jobs—with something Lakebase handles directly.

The piece notes these are hackathon projects built over about a week by eleven customer teams; it does not independently validate production performance claims beyond what was reported in testing.
items.title: Databricks Lakebase Hackathon: Branching and Sync/Serve Projects from Eleven Customer Teams

items.summary: Ton van Mol of the Dutch research institute TNO says photonic chips are on the verge of a breakthrough, and if so they could be a gamechanger. Because they use light instead of electricity, photonic chips are faster, use less energy, and generate less heat than traditional electrical computer chips, which process data by shunting electrons around tiny circuits; a single microchip produced today can contain billions of transistors with sizes measured in nanometres (one nanometre is a billionth of a metre). Van Mol hopes for an acceleration in photonics similar to the one seen in electrical chips since the 1970s, noting that 'With optical chips, you are now where electronic chips were maybe 40 [or] 50 years ago.' American, Taiwanese and Chinese firms dominate the computer chip industry, but Europe sees photonic chips as a fresh opportunity to lead on what could be a key future technology. The European Union has committed €400m ($450m; £330m) to a project called PIX Europe, with the stated goal of making the continent 'a global leader in emerging technology for Photonic Integrated Chips.' Van Mol says 'Europe said we need to have our own manufacturing in-house,' and that they cannot depend like in the past that everything is manufactured in the US or China. One part of the European Chips Act is to build pilot lines to bring photonic chip technology, which is now in labs, to the next stage - manufacturing. Electronic and photonic chips are produced on wafers made up of hundreds of individual chips, and factories with machines that can handle bigger wafers can churn out chips more efficiently. Photonic chip manufacturing worldwide is currently done on wafers four inches (10cm) in size, and the next step is to scale-up production to a six-inch wafer. Van Mol's team are already building a 10,000 sq m factory to produce six-inch indium phosphide wafers on the High Tech Campus in Eindhoven, due to fully open in 2030. 'That's the development TNO is going to do, in a pilot line which is really serious,' van Mol says. 'In 2030, we hope that we have a stable, reproducible, high-yield process, and then the intention is that the pilot line opens to industrial parties who can make commercial production out of it.' Europe has one crucial player in the current computer chip industry - ASML, the Netherlands-based tech giant which is the only company in the world able to build the machines needed to make the most sophisticated semiconductors. Van Mol says 'The way you produce these chips is very similar to the way you produce electrical or electronic chip,' because they use the same type of equipment and a high-end clean room, so the production method is very similar to traditional semiconductor technology. Stanislas Baron, head of ASML's EU/US Customer Team, says 'Europe has a strong position in photonics research. The next challenge is translating those innovations into industrial-scale manufacturing.' ASML's unique success helped build an influential and lucrative network of companies and institutions devoted to semiconductor technology in and around Eindhoven, which serves as a model for what Europe is trying to achieve with photonic chips. The Eindhoven project has the backing of former ASML chief executive Peter Wennink, author of an influential report for the Dutch government called 'The Roadmap to Future Prosperity,' which noted that the market for photonics was expected to grow 10 to 20 times in the next 10 years. In a news release backing the new pilot line, Wennink described it as 'a launchpad for Europe's future digital economy' and said 'By investing in scalable production capacity, we are creating an ecosystem that can help shape the global technological direction.' However, Europe is not alone in looking to photonic chips; in June this year US photonics company Coherent announced what it called 'the world's first and largest volume-production six-inch indium phosphide manufacturing platform' at its plant in Sherman, Texas. The expansion is backed by chip manufacturing giant Nvidia as well as $50 million public funds under the US Chips Act. Joris Teer, policy analyst at the European Institute for Security Studies in Brussels, says Europe knows that 'its high energy and labour costs, skilled workforce shortages, and lack of private and public capital make an across-the-board reindustrialisation strategy impossible,' so to retain influence, ensuring dependence on European parties rather than European autonomy is key. Once up and running, the Eindhoven project will provide a pilot production line usable by multiple companies; it will be open to businesses across Europe and beyond who can design and build chips without having to develop their own expensive production facilities. Van Mol says 'What we want to establish here is what we call a foundry model; there's no intention to have our own product,' instead producing to order for outside customers, similar to how Taiwanese-based giant TSMC has achieved global dominance in microchip manufacture at huge scale. Photonic chips are already in use in highly specialised areas such as data centres and Lidar sensor technology. For van Mol of TNO, helping the industry scale up by easing production challenges and increasing capacity is the key step to moving photonic chips into daily-life tech like phones and laptops, and driving innovation in medical scanners and 6G communications. Van Mol says 'The demand is there,' and that the end goal is manufacturing these chips in Europe because they could become 'the backbone of all data and telecom.' The article notes external links are provided for PIX Europe, Coherent, and The Roadmap to Future Prosperity report; figures such as wafer sizes (four inches/10cm current versus six-inch next step), the 2030 opening date, factory size (10,000 sq m), funding amounts (€400m/$450m/£330m for PIX Europe and $50 million under the US Chips Act), ASML's unique position as the only company able to build machines for the most sophisticated semiconductors, and photonics market growth of 10 to 20 times in the next 10 years are reported but not independently quantified here. The article frames Europe's strategy around retaining influence through dependence on European parties rather than full autonomy, which is acknowledged as a deliberate choice by analysts like Teer rather than an assertion of technological superiority.
items.title: Europe's €400m bid to lead in photonic chip manufacturing via Eindhoven pilot line

items.summary: The author describes a project exploring new ways to sandbox code executed by coding agents, with the goal of making it safer to try out local models without risking that a mistake or prompt-injection attack causes them to take damaging actions on a machine. The work was done in collaboration with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects. A post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, in which code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern, three sandbox server implementations were released: external-sandbox-v86, a Node.js server using v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly; external-sandbox-container, a Python web server running the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance; and external-sandbox-quicksand, another Python web server that uses Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package. Each implementation offers the same localhost API, allowing Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to the sandbox whenever they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy for controlling exactly which hosts the agent's code may communicate with, plus a credential replacement mechanism that enables authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent; a UI is provided for reconfiguring the proxy while the sandbox remains running. The author expresses continued fascination with safely running untrusted code and describes the external sandbox pattern as offering a neat way to experiment with different approaches.
items.title: External Sandboxes for Coding Agents

items.summary:
On 17 November 2026, OpenAI announced two new models via its Link Blog: GPT-6.2 Astra, described as a frontier model for difficult projects, and GPT-6.2 Sol, an efficient, versatile model for everyday work. Both are available in the API under gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol, with support shipped in LLM 0.38.

GPT-6.2 Astra costs $8 per million tokens input and $40 per million output — 80% of GPT-6 Astra's price (which was $10/$50) and the same as Claude Fable 5.2, also an 80% reduction from its predecessor. Its cached pricing is $0.40 per million tokens input versus $1 for the older model. GPT-6.2 Sol retains the $2/$10 price of GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Sol, which were half the cost of GPT-5.6 Sol at $4/$20.

The author provided comparison grids showing how the high/xhigh/max variants compare with previous Sol and Astra releases, ran a benchmark prompt against both models using 'Ultra' effort levels in Codex CLI to generate three.js animations of Yonkers standing up as a mech and stomping across Manhattan, Queens, and Brooklyn (using OpenStreetMap data), and produced side-by-side videos. However, the author noted that neither model morphed Yonkers into a mech well enough compared with Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon.

Reception is mixed: GPT-6.2 Astra scores lower than Claude Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and some users find its communication style confusing. A review by Theo Browne illustrates this — during a two-hour task to make an Outer Wilds level, the model became 'blocked' asking about internal implementation details such as whether r24's reviewer writes clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4.

The post also links recent articles: running a Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide (17 November 2026), locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude (9 November 2026), hiding slop PR descriptions behind something (9 November 2026), and Qwen 3.8 27B interpreting model weights on a laptop (3 November 2026).
items.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol with mixed reception

items.summary: Quaise Energy, a Houston-based startup, announced that Google has agreed to purchase up to 50 megawatts of carbon-free power from its first commercial project, Project Obsidian, located near the Newberry Volcano in central Oregon. The deal is valued at more than $500 million and would help run Google's existing data center operations in northwest Oregon as early as 2030. Quaise plans to use advanced drilling techniques and rock-melting technology to access hotter geothermal resources than traditional plants can reach, with the goal of tapping superhot rock above 572 degrees Fahrenheit. The startup said Project Obsidian will cost about $350 million to build, and it had raised $180 million in equity financing in August, including investment from Nabors Industries. Quaise is one of at least four U.S. geothermal companies that have landed agreements with tech giants for next-generation plants; Fervo Energy recently agreed to supply Google with nearly 400 megawatts from the Cape Station facility in southwest Utah, while Sage Geosystems and XGS Energy are partnering with Meta on facilities in Nevada and New Mexico respectively. Tech firms are seeking clean, around-the-clock power for their data center buildout, but these geothermal technologies have yet to be deployed widely at commercial scale, and questions remain about how effectively they will operate over long periods of time. At Project Obsidian, Quaise would initially use oil-and-gas drilling techniques to develop an enhanced geothermal system by fracturing rocks and pumping them with water to create artificial reservoirs; after drilling down some 2.5 miles it plans to switch to millimeter-wave drilling that uses high-frequency beams to melt and vaporize rock. The company is still testing this technology, having drilled through more than 330 feet of granite at its central Texas field site last year while now working toward reaching over 3,200 feet there.
items.title: Google bets on superhot geothermal to power Oregon data centers

items.summary:
Countless manure lagoons on dairy farms across California's San Joaquin Valley are vulnerable to serious flooding during what is likely a fierce and historic El Niño this winter. These pools of cow waste store slurry containing high concentrations of chloride, nitrogen, pathogens, bacteria, heavy metals, and other contaminants that can pollute the environment and nearby communities when lagoons overflow. The San Joaquin Valley has upwards of 1,000 dairy farms—the most in any part of the state—though the total number of waste lagoons statewide remains unknown.

The current El Niño is likely the strongest in over a millennium according to a recent study in Science, and will ramp up heading into December. It could bring devastating flooding that contaminates drinking water and spreads manure sludge through rural neighborhoods. This would not be the first time; record-breaking storms occurred during the 1982-83 and 1997-98 El Niños along the coast and in Southern California.

Three years ago, atmospheric rivers pummeled the San Joaquin Valley, forcing evacuation of hundreds of thousands of cows. How overflow impacted nearby communities remains unknown because a true accounting has never been completed. J. Pablo Ortiz-Partida, director of innovation and collaboration at the nonprofit Union of Concerned Scientists, noted that much of what was seen in 2023 focused on protecting cows but little addressed manure pollution. He expressed concern about families living near lagoons—many communities in central California are majority Hispanic and bear disproportionate health harms from concentrated animal feeding operations—even without flooding.

Justin Leyendekker, a dairy farmer who runs eleven farms including Hoppy Cows Dairy in Kingsburg with about 2,000 cows, counted himself lucky for not having significant damage when the region flooded in 2023. His lagoon fills to roughly 15 feet deep, and each year they drain it as low as possible; El Niño has been extra motivation to keep lagoons empty.

Lewis Bernier of Direct Action Everywhere described open pits of waste as ticking time bombs of massive pollutants and said his group is preparing response plans. Scott Hatton of the Central Valley Regional Water Quality Control Board noted water boards are providing online resources, require dairies to submit reports if discharge threatens health or environment, and encourage review of storm preparedness.

Michael Payne of UC Davis's California Dairy Quality Assurance Program wrote in an October newsletter from CARES that models predict most of the state is headed for at least 150 percent of normal rainfall. Sonia Brown noted more heat energy is being measured in the Pacific Ocean than at any time since modern recording began in 1950.

Experts suggest dairies ensure emergency plans, inspect equipment, test backup generators, handle evacuations properly, and assess flood risks based on FEMA mapping. Deanne Meyer advised keeping channels clear of debris and servicing pumps for extra hours; above-ground ponds should have space to rise at least 2 more feet and in-ground ponds 1 more foot, with adequate capacity for a '25-year, 24-hour storm event.'

Emily Miller of Food & Water Watch is concerned dairies use an old technical paper—Technical Paper No. 40 from 1961—to determine what qualifies as a '25-year storm,' which analyzes data from decades before many areas now see that intensity more often than every 25 years. Hatton said the standard remains but more recent precipitation data should be used, and dairies could use updated rainfall-frequency data under the San Joaquin Valley's dairy general order adopted in 2013.

Food & Water Watch has warned of similar risks before; in 2018, manure lagoons overflowed with 'fecal soup' spilling into neighborhoods in Iowa and North Carolina. Nobody knows how many San Joaquin Valley dairies are ready for the winter downpours, and there is no requirement for dairies to notify water board regulators about their El Niño preparations.
items.title: California Manure Lagoons Face Flooding Risk Amid Historic El Niño

items.summary: On Tuesday (Nov 17), Nvidia chair Harvey Jones stated that the board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive. items.summary:
Ruth Porat, Alphabet's longtime investment chief, acknowledged that Google — along with AI companies generally — has failed to convince US voters that the trillions of dollars being invested in data centers are worth the cost. A bipartisan backlash against data center construction galvanized voters earlier this month, who largely moved to block expansion through local measures and elected lawmakers in the midterms who mostly supported slowing the AI buildout. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta have been central to that expansion, either directly financing large projects or signing on as anchor tenants.

Porat said she has traveled extensively during this period and is hearing firsthand about affordability concerns reflected in polls: "the pain you saw reflected in polls, I'm hearing firsthand around affordability." She nonetheless argued that most Americans remain supportive of the job opportunities created by the AI boom. When discussing conversations across the country, she noted what she hears repeatedly: "This is creating opportunity that I hadn't seen in my town."

Porat also defended the dilutive and expensive capital deployment used by Alphabet and other large companies to fund their ambitions. She said, "It's expensive, but the reason we're investing is we see the extraordinary opportunity," adding, "None of us have lived at a time like this." Google is expected to spend up to $205 billion in capex this year, with even higher figures forecast for 2027. The company's free cash flow has turned negative in recent quarters, prompting investor concerns that Big Tech may be overextending itself.

In response, Porat emphasized the importance of demonstrating value alongside a strong balance sheet: "We want to make sure we're showing up with a full-stack approach that delivers value and a balance sheet that's a fortress balance sheet so that we can continue to deliver in a high-quality way."
items.title: Alphabet's Porat: AI Companies Lost Voters on Narrative and Execution

items.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has reiterated its listing requirements for Tata Sons, intensifying a dispute over the group's ownership and governance. In an November 16 letter responding to Tata Sons' October 6 request for regulatory guidance, the RBI explicitly directed compliance with Upper Layer Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC-UL) regulations, including mandatory listing. Under its Scale Based Regulation framework, entities in this classification face stricter supervision since September 2022; Tata Sons has held this status continuously and applied to surrender its Core Investment Company registration in March 2024 after repaying debt, but the RBI rejected that application in September 2026. The company's assets stood at approximately ₹2.01 lakh crore as of March 31, 2026.

The RBI's position is significant because Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata had earlier argued that the regulator's correspondence did not specifically mention listing. Former trustee Darius Khambata questioned why vice-chairmen Venu Srinivasan and Vijay Singh reversed their opposition to listing in April 2026, noting both trustees supported resolutions opposing listing in March 2024, May 2025, and July 2025. In his November 17 letter, Khambata wrote: "My grievance is why you repeatedly voted to oppose listing but suddenly did a volte face in April 2026." He also rejected allegations concerning trustee appointments and chairman N Chandrasekaran's reappointment.

Conversely, Jimmy Naval Tata—brother of late Ratan Tata—has backed an IPO while accusing Noel Tata of attempting a "back-door takeover" through family appointments. In his view: "In recent time the trusts are being filled with family members of the present Tata Trust Chairman... thereby securing a degree of control over Tata Sons that was never the settlors' intention." Jimmy Tata argued listing would strengthen accountability, transparency, and protection of the trusts' founding objectives; he opposed restructuring Tata Sons into smaller entities to avoid listing requirements as "deeply damaging and contrary to public and shareholder interests," questioned amendments concentrating power in the Trusts chairman's hands, and urged strict RBI timelines while citing TCS's successful listing under Ratan Tata.

On ownership, Tata Trusts collectively hold approximately 66% of Tata Sons, with the Shapoorji Pallonji Group holding around 18%. Listing could improve shareholder liquidity but would introduce greater disclosure requirements and market scrutiny. Although restructuring remains a possible alternative requiring RBI compliance, the central bank's latest communication reinforces the listing obligation without announcing fresh enforcement action.
items.title: RBI Reaffirms Listing Mandate for Tata Sons Amid Trusts' Opposition

items.summary: Senate Intelligence Committee member Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., demanded that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before Congress amid growing questions about his role in delaying restrictions on AI chip exports to China. Speaking with Ashley Gold at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World, Kelly said, "He needs to come to Congress," and expressed a desire to hear answers regarding why Lutnick made the decisions he did. Kelly also raised concerns about Lutnick's family business interests in the AI industry, suggesting they warranted further scrutiny from the commerce secretary. The Arizona senator argued that Lutnick should have been removed at earlier points during President Donald Trump's second term, stating there had been "multiple times" when his "expiration date in this job had already expired." Kelly additionally called for answers from Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang, who stepped down last week amid revelations about reported extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Although Huang reportedly volunteered to testify before Congress, Kelly noted that neither he nor his colleagues "have received answers" and emphasized the need for them. The senator also expressed skepticism about the Justice Department's ability to conduct an impartial investigation into the matter, citing personal experience in which he said the department had been "weaponized" against individuals — including himself over remarks reminding military personnel they must refuse unlawful orders. Kelly acknowledged his potential bias but stated he has little faith in those currently running the department. Separately, Kelly voiced support for three bipartisan provisions in the Senate's version of must-pass defense policy legislation that would strengthen export restrictions on countries of concern such as China, arguing the US must be careful about transferring its most advanced technologies. He specifically called for more "guardrails" on AI technologies and penalties for companies and individuals who violate them, noting liability "depends on the outcome," but that in cases involving particularly egregious conduct, "individuals could be held accountable."
items.title: Sen. Kelly Demands Lutnick Testify Over AI Chip Export Delays

Jensen Huang, co-founder of Nvidia and its former CEO who resigned amid unconfirmed allegations involving an extramarital affair and a purported Chinese spy relationship, has lost his blue verification tick and the Nvidia badge from his X account. A screenshot shared by a user shows these badges removed along with changes to his profile bio, which now reads only 'Founder of Nvidia.' In response to this development, Elon Musk stated that Huang's blue check would return for free on the house without requiring an X Premium subscription.

Meanwhile, discussion around Huang's potential return to Nvidia has intensified. The company's CFO Colette Kress has been appointed interim CEO while its board considers internal and external candidates for a permanent successor. Elon Musk continues to publicly support Huang; reports indicate he previously offered him a job and expressed willingness to sign a petition demanding Huang's return.

An online petition supporting Huang's return claims more than 136,000 signatures (reported as '1.36' in lakhs), though this figure has not been independently verified. Supporters reportedly include Tim Sweeney of Epic Games and Garry Tan of Y Combinator. According to a Wired report, internal support for Huang's return is also growing within Nvidia itself, with more than 1,600 comments on an internal post.

The central unresolved question remains whether Jensen Huang will once again take command of Nvidia or the company will secure a new permanent CEO.
items.title: Elon Musk Offers Free Blue Tick to Jensen Huang After Badge Removal; Return Petition Gains Support

items.summary: Nvidia reported its first quarterly results since interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress took over, with the stock climbing up to 4% in after-hours trading ahead of a scheduled analyst call at 5 p.m. ET. Net income reached $65.3 billion, up 105% from a year earlier, while Data Center revenue hit $107.6 billion, up 110% year over year and up 21% from the prior quarter. GAAP gross margin came in at 74.8%, with non-GAAP gross margin slightly higher at 74.9%. For the fourth quarter, Nvidia expects revenue of $130 billion plus or minus 3%, an outlook that excludes any Data Center compute revenue from China; this expectation exceeds the average analyst estimate of $125.1 billion per CNBC. The company also projects GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins between 71.0% and 72.0%. Nvidia reported Hopper product shipments to China totaled $2.4 billion in the quarter, noting that its Vera Rubin platform has begun shipping. Supply commitments rose to $390 billion from $279 billion in the prior quarter, driven mainly by multi-year memory procurement. The company capped guarantees tied to the SB Energy data center campus in Ohio—which will host Nvidia infrastructure leased to OpenAI—at $105 billion. Nvidia returned $28.1 billion to shareholders through buybacks and dividends; its board raised repurchase authorization by $150 billion in September, leaving $227.3 billion available, and it announced a quarterly dividend of $0.25 per share payable Dec. 23 to shareholders of record on Dec. 2. The report comes after Jensen Huang resigned last week following an admission of an affair with a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer; U.S. intelligence officials suspect she is an agent of Beijing's spy agencies. Kress assumed the interim CEO role while retaining her CFO position as the board began searching for a permanent chief executive. On governance, Nvidia established a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance on Tuesday, and Huang indicated he would be 'honored' to return as chief executive should directors conclude it is in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company, and America.
items.title: Nvidia beats earnings estimates in first report since Jensen Huang's exit

items.summary:
The Climate Change Committee (CCC) warned in a letter published Wednesday that the UK is “likely to miss” its legally binding net zero carbon emissions target of 2050 if the government proceeds with plans to relax electric vehicle sales rules. The analysis, delivered by CCC chair Nigel Topping to transport secretary Heidi Alexander, argues that weakening the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate would blow a hole in Britain’s plan and force cuts to its carbon budgets for reducing emissions. Under current rules, carmakers must sell an increasing share of electric cars each year or face fines of £12,000 per vehicle; relaxing them could add 8.4m tonnes of CO2 pollution annually by next decade. The ZEV mandate is the single biggest contributor to meeting climate goals, meaning the government would have to find other major emission reductions unless it amends its budgets to allow more pollution. Industry groups are lobbying hard to cut headline targets from 80% electric sales by 2030 down to as low as 50% or 60%, arguing the mandate places excessive financial pressure on manufacturers. Electric cars accounted for 26.6% of UK new car sales in the first 10 months of 2026, well below the 33% headline target, though carmakers are expected to meet the mandate through a series of loopholes known as “flexibilities”. Topping argued that weakening the rules would risk the government’s climate commitment, miss an opportunity to cut typical household costs by about £800 a year, increase exposure to volatile oil markets by up to 15m barrels per year in 2030, and damage long-term competitiveness as main export markets transition to electric vehicles. He added that people are buying EVs in record numbers because they are cheaper to own than alternatives, and the mandate gives supply chain businesses the certainty needed to invest while supporting thousands of jobs.

The article notes broader government concerns about meeting climate commitments: funding for heat pumps has been cut, Burnham approved gas extraction from the Jackdaw gasfield and is considering approval for the Rosebank oilfield, and MPs earlier this year voted to approve new carbon reductions for 2038-42. The Guardian reported that one cabinet minister in Keir Starmer’s government wanted to return to parliament to scrap those planned reductions in favour of a more conservative target, but the idea did not come to fruition amid opposition from other ministers. An industry source said serious consideration was still being given to changing carbon budgets ahead of Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, though it was unclear whether discussion continued; a government source strongly denied this.

The changes would also mean the UK is unlikely to meet its 2033-2037 carbon budget. Several analysts said the government will struggle to find emission reductions elsewhere given the scale of pollution from petrol and diesel cars and vans, while the policy could face opposition from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, each with their own carbon budgets. Doug Parr of Greenpeace UK criticised the Burnham government for talking climate leadership internationally while U-turning on ZEV targets at home.

The car industry rejected the CCC’s analysis. Mike Hawes of the Society for Motor Manufacturers and Traders said a successful EV transition needs a strong market and competitive industry, arguing that the CCC ignores billions in unsustainable discounts and millions more in government incentives, and that without a strong local market there is no business case to build locally.

A government spokesperson maintained commitment to phasing out all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and making all new car and van sales zero emission by 2035, adding that its consultation on the mandate would not change these goals and would take a pragmatic and balanced approach.
items.title: CCC warns UK would miss climate targets if it weakens EV sales rules

items.summary: In a statement issued Tuesday, Nvidia delivered a fiscal fourth-quarter sales forecast that exceeded Wall Street expectations, signaling continued demand following the departure of CEO Jensen Huang. The company projected Q4 revenue of $130 billion plus or minus 3%, compared with an average analyst estimate of $125.3 billion. Nvidia also raised its forward growth guidance to 75% for the next fiscal year, up from a previous forecast of 70%. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who is serving as interim CEO during Huang's exit, said in the statement that 'our momentum is real' and described Vera Rubin, the company's new chip generation, as off to 'an explosive start.' The upbeat outlook was framed against the backdrop of leadership change rather than any indication of a return by Jensen Huang. No other financial details or forward figures were provided beyond these reported estimates and guidance adjustments.
items.title: Nvidia beats revenue forecast and raises next-year growth guidance amid leadership transition

items.summary: As President Donald Trump meets Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, the fall of Nvidia's Jensen Huang has become a flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship. Beijing views the former CEO's exit as more than a personal scandal: allegations that his affair with businesswoman Alice Huang involved ties to China's Ministry of State Security have reignited Washington debate over advanced chip exports and whether the Trump administration has eased restrictions too far. The claims remain unproven, but they risk strengthening voices arguing for further limits on Chinese access to cutting-edge technology essential for AI, supercomputing, and military use. Just before the summit, the Trump administration introduced new export rules targeting firms that rent computing power in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand, or Brazil to train AI models; some of these companies, including one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips into China, though they deny it. Beijing's foreign ministry dismissed the espionage claims as a 'smear against China,' with spokesperson Mao Ning warning that the US should stop fabricating narratives to justify technological blockades, while insisting both governments have maintained close communication about their leaders' interactions. Analysts warn this could resemble the 2023 surveillance balloon incident, when Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship and diplomatic relations deteriorated sharply after a planned Blinken trip was cancelled; Global Times quoted state media comparing the Nvidia story to that episode and questioning whether someone is stirring confrontation so soon after hard-won detente. Both leaders have incentives to keep talking: China's export-reliant economy needs trade as it seeks to replace a truce expiring in January, while Trump faces an uphill domestic legislative battle after midterms and may hope for Xi's help ending the Middle East war. The summit is being staged in Shenzhen to showcase Beijing's AI ambitions, though Washington's tighter chip rules give China retaliation options through its rare earth mineral dominance, risking a cycle of economic leverage that could shift relations from engagement back toward mutual suspicion.
items.title: Nvidia spy scandal threatens Trump-Xi summit and US chip restrictions on China

items.summary: The article frames Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia as a case study in how human nature undermines cybersecurity. His departure followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China; the company stated no secrets were leaked. The author invokes Kevin Mitnick's observation that 'the human factor is truly security's weakest link' to argue that people in powerful positions repeatedly lower their defenses despite having extensive security apparatuses at their disposal. Examples cited include Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni speaking candidly about foreign affairs on a call with Russian pranksters, and former CIA Director David Petraeus giving his biographer access to classified notebooks during an affair. The author attributes these failures partly to how humans are wired to respond to other people: social cues that increase familiarity and intimacy make people feel safer, more trusting, and more willing to divulge information or take risks. Regarding the power of voice, a study conducted with social psychologist Mahdi Roghanizad found participants received about twice as many 'yes' responses when asking for favors by phone compared to email; hearing a person's voice also makes them seem more capable and relatable than reading their written thoughts. On touch, an 1984 study found servers who lightly touched diners receiving change got bigger tips, another classic study found people were 76% more likely to give change when experimenters lightly touched their arm, and a 2010 study found participants took greater financial risks after being given a comforting pat on the shoulder; researchers theorized these touches created familiarity that made people more willing to open their wallets. On face-to-face interaction, Milgram's shock experiment showed nearly two-thirds of participants administered shocks up to the highest setting when an experimenter stood behind them and gave instructions in person, versus only 22.5% when the experimenter left the room and instructed over the phone; a separate study found people were 34 times more likely to say yes to requests made in person than by email, while another study found in-person requests significantly outperformed those made over phone or video call. The author concludes that although cyberattacks and phishing emails pose real threats, some of the biggest risks come from people physically present with you, illustrating a vulnerability even robust cybersecurity measures struggle to guard against.
items.title: Jensen Huang Scandal Illustrates Why Human Nature Is Cybersecurity's Weakest Link

items.summary: Apple growers across New South Wales are reporting significantly lower yields this season, with producers suspecting a lack of feral bees—likely due to the Varroa mite—as a contributing cause. John Galbraith, who has farmed his commercial orchard in the NSW Blue Mountains for 55 years, is questioning whether he will see any fruit from his labour this year. His property on the Bells Line of Road near Bilpin holds about 3,500 apple trees and several pear trees, serving roughly 60,000 visitors annually who come largely for pick-your-own fruit. For the second consecutive season, Galbraith's trees have failed to produce much fruit despite full flowering earlier in the year; he describes it as 'a bit of a disaster,' with barely any apples or pears on his trees. In an attempt to avoid repeating last year's outcome, Galbraith brought in double the usual number of bee hives for pollination, but when opened them found few insects moving toward his orchard. He explained that growers bring hives in around 10 per cent blossom so bees become accustomed to fruit trees, yet this season 'they just seemed to head off everywhere.' Galbraith anticipates producing about 1 tonne of apples instead of the usual 40 to 50 tonnes, leaving him unable to fill commercial contracts and able to offer only up to two days of pick-your-own fruit rather than three days a week over five months. Paula Charnock, an apple grower in Orange in the state's Central West, echoed these concerns, describing it as 'very shocking' that there were no bees while flowers were in full bloom and calling the silence among her trees 'strange,' noting she had never faced such a problem before. For the first time, Charnock brought in managed hives, which produced less but well-developed fruit. Bill Shields, who farms 3,400 apple trees just 2 kilometres from Galbraith and also added extra hives to no effect, said 'there's very little commercial value left on the trees.' Growers suspect the bee shortage may relate to New South Wales' efforts against the Varroa mite. During a failed eradication attempt between 2022 and 2023, hundreds of millions of European honeybees—also called feral bees—died; these wild bees typically pollinate bushland flowers and fruit. Galbraith said that with few feral bees available, hives would naturally gravitate toward native bush flowers and fruits offering more attractive nectar and pollen rather than orchard trees. However, the NSW Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD) stated it was too early to confirm a connection. DPIRD's director of horticulture Alison Anderson said low fruit set could stem from pollination conditions but 'cannot be definitively attributed' to Varroa mite alone, listing other contributing factors including climatic conditions, varietal differences, chilling requirements, and thinning practices. To investigate the cause of reduced yields, the NSW government established a $9.5 million research fund last year. One project aims to understand pollinator communities, abundance, and diversity while comparing fruit set in crops with and without managed hives. Charnock expects prices to remain strong this season but warned that persistently low yields could affect markets if the problem continues next year.
items.title: NSW Apple Growers Report Poor Harvests Linked to Missing Bees and Varroa Mite

items.summary: On Tuesday (17 November 2026), Google stated it had found no evidence of a broad disruption to its Gmail service, even as more than 2,800 users reported email problems on the outage-tracking site Downdetector by 12 noon US Eastern Time. A Google spokesperson told Anadolu Agency that teams were monitoring service health closely and pointed to real-time updates on the Google Workspace Status Dashboard, saying: “We’re not currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption.” Most user complaints reportedly involved difficulty receiving emails, with some users reporting problems accessing the service entirely. As of 1:45 pm ET, Google’s official Workspace Status Dashboard listed no active Gmail disruptions. The reports emerged against a backdrop of several other technology failures across the US in recent days, including an outage affecting Microsoft’s Outlook email service and a telecommunications failure that led the Federal Aviation Administration to temporarily halt flights nationwide. Google indicated there is no evidence linking the reported Gmail problems to those separate incidents. The article was published by Rabia Iclal Turan of Anadolu Agency, with an update posted on 17 November 2026 from Washington.
items.title: Google denies widespread Gmail outage amid thousands of user reports

items.summary: Pauline Hanson of the rightwing party One Nation announced on Tuesday a hardline migration plan that would cut Australia's annual refugee intake from 20,000 places per year to 2,000 and abolish the permanent parent visa program. She labelled the approach 'tough' and claimed it would still leave Australia above the OECD average for places per capita, though she acknowledged this would end the country's status as one of the most generous refugee programs behind Canada. Hanson argued that the taxpayer cost is enormous, citing an average lifetime expenditure of about $500,000 per person in-country, and said her plan would save more than $140bn over 10 years based on Treasury modelling adjusted for inflation. That analysis put the lifetime cost of a humanitarian entrant at $523,000; earlier December 2021 Treasury modelling had found the cost to be $400,000 with 90% borne by the federal government. Hanson framed her concern around people who cannot fund their own bed or hospital beds and said she was worried about those 'doing it tough.' The plan would keep banned migrants from countries on Albanese government's 'do not travel' list—including Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Somalia—out of the country. Under One Nation, migrant parents could still move to Australia but only if sponsored by family rather than taxpayers, or they could visit relatives on temporary visas; Hanson said the party was not barring them from entering. Labor has committed to retaining the intake at 20,000 per year while the Coalition promised to halve it to 10,000. Foreign minister Penny Wong accused One Nation of trying to divide the country and questioned whether Australia would remain above the OECD average under Hanson's plan. Wong said she did not accept those figures and argued that with unprecedented global displacement—the most human beings displaced since world war II—Australia makes only a small contribution through its refugee intake, which she called 'the right balance.' She dismissed One Nation as 'more of the same,' saying they believe dividing Australians is the best political response. Wong noted other nations including the US and Canada have tightened their migration programs recently, with Canada reducing its parent visa program.
items.title: One Nation vows to slash Australia's refugee intake by 90% and scrap permanent parent visas

items.summary: Tiger Woods will tee it up at next month's Hero World Challenge, ending more than two years away from official competition. The event takes place in the Bahamas and is hosted by Woods himself as a 20-player tournament. He has not competed in a world-ranking tournament since missing the cut at the 2024 British Open due to injuries, surgeries, and legal complications. The Hero World Challenge is a 72-hole event with no cut. Woods underwent surgery to repair a nerve impingement on his lower back in September 2024, then ruptured his Achilles tendon in March 2025 while training at home—an injury that forced him to miss the 2025 season—and had another operation in October 2025 to replace a disc in his lower back. His comeback attempt was also derailed when he was arrested in March on a misdemeanor driving under the influence charge after a rollover crash in Florida. Woods accepted a five-year suspension of his driver's license in September after reaching a deal with prosecutors, and has largely remained out of the public eye since then, even spending time outside the U.S. to seek treatment and focus on his health. He joins the Hero World Challenge field as one of three exemptions along with Rickie Fowler and 2019 U.S. Open champion Gary Woodland. Woods announced his return on Instagram, posting photos of the three golfers who will round out this year's field. The December 3-6 charity event that benefits Woods' foundation is not an official tournament on the PGA Tour schedule but does receive world ranking points. World number one Scottie Scheffler, who won Hero World Challenge titles in 2023 and 2024, headlines this year's field. In total, six of the current top 10 in the world are among those competing, a group that also includes Matt Fitzpatrick, Cameron Young, Chris Gotterup, Xander Schauffele, and Sam Burns.
items.title: Tiger Woods to make competitive return at December's Hero World Challenge

items.summary:
The minor party One Nation has announced a plan to cut Australia's annual refugee intake from 20,000 places to 2,000 — an approximately 90 per cent reduction — while eliminating the visa program for parents of migrants. Party leader Pauline Hanson framed the move as "tough love" and argued that although Australia was "built on migration," it could no longer "afford it." The refugee proposal builds on a September net-negative migration policy, which sought to cut 750,000 temporary visa holders over three years before capping annual net overseas migration at 130,000. Hanson said scrapping parent visas and most of the humanitarian intake would reduce Australia's migration spend by $100 billion over a decade, drawing on Treasury data through One Nation analysis; she declined to have it costed by the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO), arguing that office only models about a year and that long-term modelling is not feasible. Under her plan, parents of migrants already in Australia on bridging visas — numbering around 157,000 — would receive an application fee refund but ultimately face leaving unless they secure another pathway to stay. The current scheme caps parent and aged parent visa grants each financial year at 8,500, compared with 7,060 the previous year; under One Nation's proposal, sponsors could still bring parents via the sponsoring parent program. Hanson also reiterated longstanding party commitments to withdraw Australia from the UN Refugee Convention and reinstate temporary protection visas, arguing that a 90 per cent cut would remain above other OECD countries' average per capita intake.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong disputed One Nation's framing, saying Australia made only "a very small contribution" to global refugee intake and that its current level represented "the right balance." She characterized scrapping parent visas as "very harsh" while affirming a duty to accept refugees. The article notes other political positions: in August Prime Minister Anthony Albanese intervened against speculation of reducing the intake from 20,000 to 13,750; the Coalition has pledged to halve it to 10,000; and Labor recently scaled back planned backpacker visa cuts after industry warnings. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke maintained government commitment to its 225,000 net overseas migration figure.
items.title: One Nation proposes cutting refugee intake by 90 per cent and scrapping parent visas

items.summary: On Nov. 16, a group of roughly 20 Indigenous Awá people living in voluntary isolation approached an Indigenous Guajajara village in the northeastern Maranhão state of Brazil. The encounter has drawn attention from Indigenous peoples and activists concerned about the safety of the Awá, who are considered the most threatened isolated group on the planet. The motivation for the contact remains unclear; however, Guajajara leaders reportedly expressed concern over the physical condition of some members—especially children and older people—who appeared very thin. According to accounts and images posted by Indigenous organizations on social media, the Guajajara offered the Awá food and other objects before the group returned briefly to the forest. Brazil's Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, told Mongabay that technical teams are monitoring the situation and had activated a contingency plan to ensure relevant agencies can respond appropriately regarding ethno-environmental protection, health, safety, and respect for the peoples' right to self-determination. Sarah Shenker, director and senior researcher at Survival International Brazil, noted this is the first time in decades that the Awá of the Arariboia Indigenous Territory have made such close contact with other people. She added concern because the encounter occurred during November, one of the main inhabited periods when the Awá typically have more water and animals to hunt; she said they appeared to be asking for yams and some observers suggested hunger drove them out—though it is impossible to know exactly why without hearing directly from the Awá, which may never happen. Shenker emphasized that these peoples have very little resistance to diseases, so anything caught during contact could be fatal. Activists say the episode underscores the need to strengthen public policies for Indigenous protection and ensure adopted measures prioritize their lives and safety; Coapima stated protecting isolated Indigenous peoples means guaranteeing their right to live in their territories while preserving their ways of life, choices, and existence. The banner image shows uncontacted Awá people on Nov. 16, 2026, courtesy of the Guajajara Indigenous people via Survival International.
items.title: Isolated Awá People's Rare Contact with Guajajara Village Raises Health and Safety Concerns in Brazil

items.summary: The article 'Assignment Asia: The Surgeon Across the Border' frames a broader theme in which countries and individuals across Asia are working together to realize shared dreams, with personal stories used to explore how technology, cooperation, and a belief in sharing progress are reshaping the continent. It notes that today's technology is increasingly deployed to offer life-changing solutions and promote greater convenience. In medicine specifically, China and Thailand are described as pioneering a new way of connecting specialized doctors with patients who urgently need care through high-speed internet connections and robot arms. The piece illustrates this by describing a Thai cancer patient undergoing surgery while his doctor prepares to conduct the complex procedure from three thousand kilometers away in China. This arrangement is presented as bridging unequal access to doctors, made possible through advanced technology and greater cooperation between the two countries. No specific individuals, institutions, dates, or technical specifications are named beyond these general assertions; the account remains at the level of reported framing rather than detailed operational description.
items.title: Assignment Asia: The Surgeon Across the Border

items.summary:
Jason Clay, an anthropologist who spent more than three decades at the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), has died of complications following a stem-cell transplant at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore. He was born in 1951 and grew up near King City, Missouri, as one of seven children on a small farm where his family lived on less than a dollar per person per day; he drove a tractor by age three and hunted and fished for food from age seven. His father died in a tractor accident when Clay was 15, after which he helped run the farm. He had dyslexia, did not rank among the top students at high school, and was discouraged from public speaking before a scholarship took him to Harvard; he later studied at the London School of Economics and earned a doctorate in anthropology from Cornell.

Clay’s environmental work began when, in 1988, he attended a Grateful Dead concert at Madison Square Garden and met Ben Cohen of Ben & Jerry’s. Clay suggested developing an ice cream flavor using nuts gathered from tropical forests on the theory that higher payments for forest products might give people reason to keep trees standing. Within a year, Rainforest Crunch reached supermarket shelves; Clay then set up a trading company and worked with more than 50 businesses across some 200 products, generating roughly $100 million in retail sales at one point buying around a fifth of the world’s Brazil nuts while paying gatherers two or three times the going rate. He later called Rainforest Crunch a failure because ranchers and loggers had little reason to change their practices; he said “We were attacking the wrong driver” and should have focused on beef, lumber and soy.

At WWF, which he joined in 1993, Clay sought to reduce environmental damage by influencing major agricultural commodity buyers and establishing sustainability standards. In a 2010 TED talk he calculated that just 100 companies handled a quarter of the trade in 15 commodities WWF had identified as major threats to biodiversity, with names like Cargill appearing repeatedly across different commodities; he wanted rivals such as Coca-Cola and Pepsi or Cargill and Bunge to agree on environmental rules while competing elsewhere through “precompetitive collaboration.” When WWF helped convene discussions for farmed-salmon sustainability standards, three of the eight original participants sued one another before meetings expanded to include producers accounting for about 60% of the world’s farmed salmon. WWF later helped establish similar standards for sugar and soy.

Clay grew increasingly critical of voluntary certification schemes he had helped create. He argued that shoppers could not tell how a product was made in seconds, that standards often became “Christmas trees” as more requirements were added and drove up costs while better producers got undercut by less responsible competitors, and that such schemes depended on companies wanting to do the right thing; “Most probably don’t,” he said in a 2024 WWF interview. In his final years he promoted Codex Planetarius, a proposal for minimum environmental standards for food entering international trade, and proposed a 1% insurance premium on exports of key food commodities to help least-efficient producers change methods.

Clay met his wife Mary Ann Mills at a castle in the Scottish Highlands belonging to Anita and Gordon Roddick; they spent 34 years together and raised three children in Arlington, Virginia. In May WWF’s board honored him for more than 30 years of service, during which he spoke about ideas that had waited long for support: 13 years for Codex Planetarius and 33 for the 1% Fund; when asked how his program could achieve ten times results in three years rather than doubling them in a year, Clay suggested its impact might double within a year. During his illness he continued holding meetings and raising money for WWF’s food and markets work before dying at Johns Hopkins Hospital following complications from a stem-cell transplant after which both his sons had been donors.

Reflecting on his rise from rural poverty, Clay pointed to government programs and scholarships that helped him while noting “I’m not under any illusion that every poor kid in the US could have done what I did,” adding that plenty could have given the chance. His family established a scholarship in his name for a low-income graduating senior from King City High School.
items.title: Jason Clay: from rural poverty to persuading big business on sustainability dies aged 75

items.summary: This edition of The Hub frames a stronger Asia-Pacific community as beginning with mutual understanding and direct connections between people. Editor Wang Guan introduces two longtime China residents to share personal perspectives on how lived experience can challenge misconceptions and how education and people-to-people exchanges build cross-regional understanding. Michael Crook, British-Canadian born in Beijing in 1951, represents a multigenerational family connection with China. Mark Levine is an American sociologist, educator, and singer-songwriter who has spent 20 years in the country. The two are brought together to discuss how their personal experiences can challenge misconceptions about one another's societies and how education and people-to-people exchanges contribute to mutual understanding across the Asia-Pacific. Their contributions reflect individual lived experience rather than any stated policy positions, official assessments, or measurable outcomes of APEC engagement that appear in the source material. The framing rests on the premise that personal connection is a foundation for broader regional community building, though specific arguments and conclusions drawn by Crook and Levine are not detailed beyond their introduction as participants in this exchange. No quantitative data, statistics, dates, or programmatic details about APEC itself are provided in the item beyond its thematic title reference to an 'APEC moment.' The document therefore conveys a qualitative invitation to dialogue rather than reporting on concrete events, agreements, or measurable results associated with APEC gatherings.
items.title: APEC: Connecting People Across the Asia-Pacific Through Personal Experience

items.summary: Nvidia reported fourth-quarter financial results on Tuesday that exceeded Wall Street expectations, offering investors some relief following the departure of longtime leader Jensen Huang. The company forecast quarterly revenue between $130 billion plus or minus 3%, above analysts' average estimate of $125.25 billion per LSEG data, and expects adjusted gross margin at 71% to 72%, versus an analyst estimate of 71.7%. Nvidia's outlook assumes no data-center chip sales to China. The company is valued at roughly $3.8 trillion; its shares rose nearly 4% in extended trading but remained down about 17% for the year through Tuesday's close. Interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress said, "Our momentum is real," without addressing leadership uncertainty, noting that Vera Rubin was off to an explosive start with a roadmap on track. Huang resigned Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees. US intelligence agencies are assessing the extent of Alice Huang's ties to China's Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing. Huang's exit ended three decades of founder-led control over Nvidia's chip roadmap, customer deals, and Washington ties, leading analysts to view execution as a bigger risk than near-term AI demand. The board is considering internal and external candidates for the CEO role; although it is not currently considering Huang's return, he said Tuesday he would be "honored" to return if deemed best by the board. A growing Stand With Jensen campaign has complicated the search. Earlier on Tuesday, Nvidia created a committee on national security and export controls as its first major governance move since Huang's departure, amid rising scrutiny of the chipmaker's national security role. Washington has tightened licensing rules for chip shipments to Southeast Asia and overseas data centers serving Chinese firms, while lawmakers prepare to question Huang, who had advocated greater chip exports to China. Investors remain uneasy about AI spending after Democrats' midterm sweep fueled fears of tougher scrutiny and slower data-center expansion; they also want clarity on whether the next CEO will continue financing customers, a practice critics call circular. Tuesday's results provided an early read on Vera Rubin, Nvidia's newest generation of AI processors succeeding Grace Blackwell. The company said in August that Vera Rubin would account for about one-fifth of data-center revenue in the October quarter and forecast 70% revenue growth over the next fiscal year. In its third quarter, Nvidia reported revenue more than doubling to $115.84 billion, beating analysts' estimate of $109.11 billion; adjusted gross margin rose to 74.9% from 73.5% a year earlier, also above the analyst estimate of 74.1%, despite soaring memory prices and production ramps. Nvidia has topped Wall Street's revenue expectations for 17 straight quarters. The article was published on November 18, 2026, per Reuters; it does not quantify billions invested in cloud providers, suppliers, or AI startups beyond qualitative framing of investor scrutiny over Huang's exit.
items.title: Nvidia beats revenue estimates amid leadership uncertainty after Jensen Huang's resignation

On Tuesday, Amazon announced plans to invest an additional $7 billion (7,000,000,000 dollars) in renewable energy projects across India by 2030. This new commitment builds on the company's existing portfolio of contracted Indian projects valued at $4 billion (4,000,000,000 dollars), positioning Amazon among India's leading corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy. The investment is intended to support what the company describes as a transition toward a more sustainable and resilient energy future in the country.

The announcement comes amid rapid growth in data centre demand for power. Industry estimates place current pipeline data centre capacity at over 5GW (5 gigawatts), while existing installed capacity stands below 2GW (2 gigawatts). Government projections suggest that national capacity could rise to between 24 and 26GW within the next five years, a surge expected to intensify demand for reliable power and make renewable energy access increasingly important for operators.

Amazon said all major global hyperscalers and leading Indian data centre operators have signed binding renewable energy commitments. Separately, Google has secured a power distribution licence in Andhra Pradesh for its AI data centre hub. Within Amazon's existing $4 billion portfolio of contracted projects, the company announced four new utility-scale wind and solar developments with a combined capacity of 934MW (934 megawatts). These include a 234MW (234 megawatts) wind farm in Bijapur, Karnataka; a 200MW (200 megawatts) hybrid solar and wind project in Tumkur — both developed by Sunsure Energy; a 300MW (300 megawatts) solar project in Mandsaur, Madhya Pradesh, to be developed by Waree; and a 200MW (200 megawatts) solar project in Dinkar, Rajasthan.

Amazon stated that the Indian investments would contribute toward its new global goal of reducing the carbon intensity of electricity powering its operations by 65% by 2030. New and renewable energy minister Pralhad Joshi said such investments play an important role in advancing India's clean energy ambitions, strengthening energy security, and supporting sustainable economic growth, while also demonstrating growing confidence among global companies in India's renewable sector. Kara Hurst, Amazon's chief sustainability officer, described the commitments as reflecting years of sustained effort, planning, and collaboration across the industry.
items.title: Amazon commits $7 billion to renewable energy in India by 2030

items.summary:
Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones announced Tuesday that the board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, a decision made hours after Huang posted on social media that he would return if the board deemed it in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company, and the country. This was Huang's first public statement since abruptly leaving last week following revelations of an extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. In his post, Huang acknowledged making 'serious mistakes' in his personal life but said he had received an 'outpouring' of support from employees, investors, business partners, and customers.

Support for reinstatement has come from several prominent figures: SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, along with President Donald Trump — a frequent ally who spoke with Huang regularly. Trump suggested Monday that the ex-CEO could return, noting he 'learned a big lesson' and 'would certainly not mind' if Huang were reinstated.

A petition titled 'Stand with Jensen,' launched last week, has gained momentum among current and former Nvidia staff, investors, and Silicon Valley supporters. Its organizers issued an open letter stating they are concerned that 'Jensen was removed without meaningful due process' and that no evidence substantiating the spy allegation had been shown.

Notably, Nvidia's third-quarter earnings statement released Tuesday made no mention of Huang's ouster or possible return. Despite the turmoil, revenue exceeded $116 billion — double the prior year — with net income of $2.70 per share versus estimates of $2.48. Data center segment revenue more than doubled to $107.6 billion, and full-year guidance for the quarter through January was set at $130 billion.

Separately, key House lawmakers announced that Huang has agreed to appear for transcribed congressional interviews on Dec. 1, followed by Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter on Dec. 2. The three overseeing committees stated they look forward to hearing about 'a potential breach of our national security' and the role of a possible Chinese intelligence asset in the scandal.

In response to the revelations, Nvidia is creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance — a move Trump called 'good.' Huang's affair involved Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based firm under U.S. investigation for allegedly diverting advanced AI chips to China.
items.title: Nvidia Board Rejects Jensen Huang's Return as CEO Amid AI Chip Scandal and Record Earnings

His departure drew support from Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and President Donald Trump, while an online petition calling for his reinstatement has gathered backing from employees, investors, and Silicon Valley figures who questioned whether due process was followed and demanded an independent investigation.

items.title: Nvidia Chairman Rules Out Jensen Huang's Return as Revenue Doubles in Q3

items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged that the tech industry's approach to building data centers has failed to win public support, speaking at a conference in Menlo Park on Monday. He said there is 'plenty of room to build' given the country's size and space, but conceded that 'the current way they're working, being built, and the engagement with communities is not working for people,' adding that 'The ecosystem will adapt.' Altman made these remarks at the inaugural Silicon Valley and the World summit hosted by Semafor near Sand Hill Road. He framed data centers as a visible symbol of AI's broader ambitions, noting they are 'like a big physical instantiation of this broader thing.' If society must trade away its agency in exchange for benefits like curing cancer or cheaper products, Altman called that 'a terrible sales pitch,' warning people would 'lose all agency and control and voice in the future.' The comments came nearly two weeks after US midterms produced around 40 new measures restricting or banning data center development. Analyst Dan Ives now estimates that 10 percent of the 800 to 1,000 planned US data centers will not be built as a result. AFP reported on these statements and their context for this item.
items.title: Altman Acknowledges Public Anger Over Data Center Builds

items.summary: The leaders of the Quad—Australia's PM Anthony Albanese, India's PM Narendra Modi, Japan's PM Sanae Takaichi, and US President Donald Trump—met in Manila on Tuesday for the first summit of the grouping in two years. The meeting came amid doubts not about the Quad's survival but about the level at which it will function. Trump described the Quad as 'very important and special' and praised Modi as 'a friend and a great leader,' while announcing that the Quad would conduct its first military exercise featuring maritime patrol aircraft in March 2027, working to protect 'peace through strength.' The leaders expressed grave concern over economic coercion, including through arbitrary export curbs, and committed to ensuring open, safe and resilient maritime transit corridors in the Indo-Pacific. Modi said for India the Quad is a trusted partnership, adding that from maritime security to trusted supply chains, new technologies to disaster response, it has been their endeavour that the Quad provides trusted solutions for the entire Indo-Pacific. The short joint press release—unlike the expansive 2024 Wilmington Declaration—cut Beijing some slack by not explicitly mentioning the South or East China Sea. With India unable to host the summit for the past two years, Modi pitched a meeting in early 2027; there was no acknowledgement of the next summit in the joint release. The statement strongly opposed any 'destabilising or unilateral actions that seek to change the status quo, including by force or coercion, which escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability.' Notably, the meeting took place hours before Trump's departure for China, where he is set to attend a potentially landmark trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin. Trump said Quad nations had reached several new critical mineral deals to secure their supply chains and ensure that none of them remained vulnerable to coercion by any single foreign supplier. The joint statement noted that P-8 and P-3C patrol aircraft are scheduled to fly in a maritime exercise for the first time in a Quad context, 'making our seas safer,' with the exercise taking place in Guam next year under the Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration—an initiative launched in May this year to enhance information sharing and maritime domain awareness. The statement unequivocally condemned terrorism and violent extremism in all its forms and manifestations, including cross-border terrorism, and committed to strengthening the Quad's ongoing cooperation on counterterrorism. It also said that the Quad is working to secure critical supply chains, protect freedom of navigation and overflight, drive growth through technologies of the future—including investments and deployment of trusted AI—and respond to disasters with life-saving assistance. AI was a major area of focus, with leaders backing the AI Accelerator, announced by foreign ministers on the margins of the G20 meeting in Atlanta, intended to coordinate and fund efforts to support trusted AI access and technical assistance across the Indo-Pacific. Foreign secretary Vikram Misri said the Quad leaders agreed to launch a business forum bringing together businesses, academics and industries to foster greater business ties across private sectors, including promoting commercial deals and partnerships critical to the prosperity of the Indo-Pacific.
