items.summary: According to a person aware of the developments told Economic Times (ET), Bain Capital–backed RSB Group is contemplating filing its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) next month—December—and the proposed issue size is likely around ₹4,000 crore. The company has appointed Axis Capital, Jefferies and HSBC Securities and Capital Markets as book-running lead managers for the issue. In the run-up to the proposed issue, five new investors collectively bought less than 10% of the company; these include White Oak Capital (promoted by former Goldman Sachs executive Prashant Khemka), JM Financial, 360One Asset, Abakkus Four2Eighth opportunities fund and Novaa One. The Behera family—RSB Group's promoters—also participated in the round, providing additional capital to the company. Bain Capital struck a partnership with RSB Group in 2024 but has not disclosed the size of its stake. RSB operates 19 manufacturing plants in India and two in Mexico, serving Tier-I customers across India and the US, and manufactures precision-engineered drivetrain components for commercial vehicles, passenger cars, construction equipment and agricultural machinery—including propeller shafts, axle systems, gears and gearboxes, clutches and construction equipment aggregates. The article notes that details are based on a single source aware of developments, with Bain's stake size undisclosed.
items.title: Bain-backed RSB Group plans Rs 4,000 crore IPO; DRHP likely in December

items.summary: The BSE Sensex rose 427.40 points, or 0.52%, to close at 82,532.19, while the NSE Nifty gained 96.30 points, or 0.38%, settling at 25,387.40. Both benchmarks ended on their highest closing levels since February 2026, recovering from losses incurred during the initial phase of a West Asia conflict linked to an Iran-US crisis that had triggered sharp global selloffs. Banking stocks led the sectoral rally: the Nifty PSU Bank index jumped nearly 2% and the Nifty Private Bank index rose around 1%. The Nifty Realty index also gained nearly 2%, while the Nifty Auto and several other sectoral indices advanced around 1%. Among individual gainers on the Sensex, Axis Bank, Reliance Industries, State Bank of India, TCS and Adani Ports each rose roughly 2%. Conversely, HCL Technologies, Power Grid, Tech Mahindra and Infosys declined up to 2%.
items.title: Sensex and Nifty reach nine-month highs on bank-led rally as FPIs drive gains amid DII selling

items.summary: The Indian rupee rose sharply on Tuesday, piercing the psychologically significant 93.50 level against the dollar as it reached a seven-month high despite an overall surge in the U.S. dollar index. The dollar index climbed nearly 2% in a month to hit its highest point in 19 months, trading at a fresh peak of 103.70 on Tuesday according to Dow Jones MarketWatch data; a reading above 100 indicates relative dollar firmness against a basket of major global currencies. The rupee's ascent was driven primarily by strong foreign investment flows into Indian equities rather than weakness in the dollar alone, with month-to-date inflows through November tracking at a record $10 billion as foreign investors poured money into local stocks. Domestic equity benchmarks eclipsed all losses made since the start of the Iran war on February 27, riding these nearly $10 billion of recent foreign fund inflows. Falling crude oil prices also buoyed the currency; crude fell to around $92 a barrel from $95 the previous day, helping mitigate concerns over India's import bill and external balances. Three institutions - Goldman Sachs, State Bank of India, and the International Energy Agency - have forecast cooler oil prices for the rest of the year, increasing the probability of further rupee appreciation. Anil Bhansali, head of treasury at Finrex Treasury Advisors, noted that AI trade money has been the main flow into India, which is good news for importers but means exporters will now have to hedge their near-term requirements. The local unit was 25 paise stronger from its previous close of 93.72, trading between 93.39 and 93.74 on a day when Taiwanese, Thai, and South Korean equity gauges each retreated nearly 2%. Bhansali also pointed to good dollar sales by foreign banks around 93.58 levels as indicating an appreciation bias for the currency. The rupee has gained 3.7% from record low levels of 96.96 hit in late May, and a senior trader from a public sector bank said it looks like 95-96 levels will take some time to return because exporters sell dollars and hedge as soon as the rupee appreciates, creating what they describe as a healthy balance.
items.title: Indian Rupee Climbs to 7-Month High Amid Dollar Strength and Falling Oil Prices

As the BJP faces growing scrutiny over its development, investment and law-and-order claims in Uttar Pradesh ahead of the 2027 polls, Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath is increasingly reverting to electoral polarisation built on the state's Hindu-Muslim population divide. Analysts interpret this shift as a retreat from performance-based politics toward identity politics, which helped the BJP seize power from the Samajwadi Party in 2017 and win its second consecutive term in 2022. Sharat Pradhan argues that if Vajpayee's development model collapsed in the 2004 India Shining debacle, then Yogi's government lacks a credible enough record to rely on governance alone; with intense pushback from voters including core supporters, polarisation is seen as its time-tested electoral weapon.

The growth narrative faces mounting challenges. Analyst Pramod Goswami points to recurring infrastructure failures that have raised questions about the model: in June 2024 parts of Ayodhya's 13-km Ram Path caved in after pre-monsoon showers, with the Public Works Department blaming hurried construction; and the Ganga Expressway developed a 10-metre-deep crater barely four months after its inauguration. Goswami notes that people have been releasing videos online to flag concerns over poor construction quality, road safety hazards and structural issues.

The infrastructure overhaul has also carried human costs. In Ayodhya, widening the Ram Path, Bhakti Path and Ram Janmabhoomi Path reportedly affected 4000 shops and residential establishments according to the city's traders' association; the Kashi Vishwanath Corridor led to loss of hundreds of homes and commercial properties.

Experts also describe growing resentment over what political analyst Shashikant Pandey calls the corporatisation of spirituality, where big companies built lavish farmhouses and resorts that drove up property prices. Analyst Anand Vardhan adds that many awarded companies lacked capacity for big-ticket projects and a large chunk went to the Gujarat lobby, fueling resentment among local developers.

On investment claims, CM Yogi has repeatedly cited figures running into millions of dollars; over 10 years he claimed more than Rs 38 lakh crore attracted across sectors, with nearly Rs 3 lakh crore in proposals through 31 MoUs signed at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January 2026. However, the state's Nivesh Sarathi portal shows that against MoUs worth nearly Rs 38.7 lakh crore, only about Rs 3.75 lakh crore of projects have commenced commercial operations — less than 10% of claimed investments; and only a third reached ground-breaking.

On law and order, Yogi's tough-on-crime image rests on police encounters, bulldozer action and enforcement drives, but NCRB data for 2024 show UP recorded the highest crimes against women nationally at 66396 cases and the most atrocities against Scheduled Castes at 14642. Its dowry death rate stood at 1.8, more than twice the national average of 0.8.

The Allahabad High Court flagged prolonged delays in investigations and accused police of total lethargy and inaction; on November 3 it termed civil liberties 'shameful,' saying violations appeared routine for police. Analyst Goswami argues that after a decade, there is nobody left to blame, perception management works only up to a point, and rising atrocities against Dalits and women have made the government uneasy about whether its law-and-order rhetoric will convince voters.

Analysts conclude that discontent over infrastructure failures, displacement, unfulfilled investment promises and persistent crimes has made it harder for the BJP to rely on governance alone. The SP-Congress PDA coalition under Akhilesh Yadav is expanding and making inroads into BJP's traditional base; Vardhan says the revival of the 80-20 formula aims to move discourse away from delivery toward religious polarisation, consolidating Hindu support while countering the SP's social coalition. The party's internal surveys and RSS feedback reportedly paint a gloomy electoral picture.
items.title: BJP's Return to Hindutva Polarisation in UP Ahead of 2027 Polls

A legal battle is unfolding within India's TVS industrial family over who controls businesses, holds shares, and benefits from the group's wealth. On November 16, Lakshmi Venu formally sought a partition of her father Venu Srinivasan's branch joint-family assets, asking him to ensure a fair and lawful division while discharging his fiduciary duties as head of family. Her mother Mallika Srinivasan publicly backed the claim; she heads Tractors and Farm Equipment Limited (TAFE), the flagship tractor maker of the Chennai-based Amalgamations Group. The dispute pits Lakshmi against her father Venu Srinivasan and brother Sudarshan Venu, raising questions about inheritance, beneficial ownership, and control across one of India's prominent business groups.

Lakshmi's claim covers family interests held through the VS Trust and other holding structures, including stakes in TVS Holdings, TVS Motor Company, TVS Credit Services, and Sundaram-Clayton, as well as businesses and assets allotted to Venu Srinivasan's branch under the broader 2020 TVS family arrangement. She contends that while the 2020 arrangement divided business segments and management responsibilities, it did not ensure a fair distribution of the family's economic interests or amount to a complete partition within the Srinivasan family.

Venu Srinivasan and Sudarshan Venu maintain that businesses and assets have already been divided through the 2020 arrangement, arguing that Venu is entitled to decide how his own assets are distributed. The distinction between management control and economic ownership lies at the heart of the dispute, according to senior journalist K Giriprakash, who has followed the matter.

The complexity deepens because family interests are held through a network of companies and trust structures rather than directly by individuals. Per Giriprakash, the VS Trust holds nearly 67 per cent in TVS Holdings and 46.83 per cent in Sundaram Clayton, while TVS Holdings owns around 56 per cent of TVS Motor. These layered shareholding links show how control and economic interests can be distributed across several ownership levels.

In April 2025, TVS Holdings disclosed Sudarshan Venu as a significant beneficial owner through the family trust structure. Giriprakash noted that declaring a significant beneficial owner is not the same as transferring registered share ownership, underscoring the distinction between who benefits and who legally holds shares.

Lakshmi's position also invokes the Hindu Succession Act of 1956 and its 2005 amendment. The law recognises daughters as coparceners in a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF), granting them equal rights to ancestral or joint family property, while the Supreme Court's 2020 judgment in Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma clarified that a daughter acquires coparcenary rights by birth regardless of whether her father was alive on September 9, 2005. However, Giriprakash cautioned that these provisions establish daughters' equal rights in coparcenary property but do not automatically confer ownership over every company or business associated with the family; application depends on how assets are held and legally characterised.

Venu and Sudarshan's likely defence rests on arguing that the 2020 arrangement already divided relevant businesses and assets, so Venu is entitled to decide distribution of his property. The distinction between ancestral and self-acquired property could be central: if specific assets are established as Venu's self-acquired property, coparcenary claims would differ from those concerning ancestral or joint family property. Trust documents governing the trusts, beneficiary identities, and attached rights may also determine whether Lakshmi's claims hold.

Giriprakash compared the case to the earlier Murugappa dispute, where women members sought greater roles in business and decision-making; but he noted the two are not identical because Lakshmi already holds an important role in TVS. The central question is therefore less about her place in management than whether the family's division of assets adequately recognised her economic and beneficial interests.

Ultimately, Giriprakash said this is a contest over how wealth, beneficial ownership, and control are distributed between two siblings with their parents taking opposite sides. The outcome will depend on the terms of the 2020 arrangement, the source and legal character of the assets, trust documents, and ownership structures involved.
